\begin{document}
\title{Ellheegner4d: A Computational Tool for Computing Generators of Rank
1 Elliptic Curves Using Heegner Points and 4-Descent}
\author{Deping Huang xiaohengdao@gmail.com}
\maketitle

\section*{Abstract}

This paper introduces a computational tool designed for computing
the generators of rank 1 elliptic curves. Based on a slightly modified
version of Pari/GP, the tool adopts a combined method of Heegner points
and 4-descent, which can effectively accelerate the computation of
generators. The above computational process is derived from Watkins'
work in 2006, and the computation of 4-descent makes use of the online
Magma computational tool. In particular, it should be noted that we
have used this tool to compute the generator of an elliptic curve
with a canonical height of 47349. The code of this paper has been
open-sourced on the GitHub platform.

\section{Introduction}

Computing generators is a fundamental and essential task in the study
of elliptic curves, yet this process is generally fraught with notable
computational challenges in practice. Fortunately, for elliptic curves
of rank 1, the Heegner point method \cite{gross_heegner_1986,goos_heegner_1994}
offers a viable approach to calculate non-torsion points on the curve
and further verify its generators. The computational efficiency of
the Heegner point method for generator calculation hinges on two key
factors: the conductor $N$ of the curve and the canonical height
$h$ of the generator. 

For elliptic curves with moderately sized $N$ and $h$ --- for instance,
$N<e^{20}$ and $h<10^{3}$, the $\texttt{ellheegner}$ function in
Pari/GP \cite{pari_gp} can typically yield results within minutes,
tens of minutes, or a few hours on modern general-purpose computer
hardware. In contrast, for curves with a canonical height $h>2\times10^{4}$
, the $\texttt{ellheegner}$ function proves to be extremely time-consuming.
As a concrete example, the author of this paper computed the generator
of an elliptic curve with $h\approx27444$ and $N\approx e^{17.25}$
on a personal computer equipped with a 13th-generation Intel Core
i5 CPU, which took a total of 76 hours to complete. This clearly demonstrates
that the direct application of the Heegner point method results in
very low computational efficiency for elliptic curves with higher
canonical heights. 

In 2006, Watkins \cite{watkins_remarks_2006} proposed an improved
approach that combined the Heegner point method with the 4-descent
method \cite{balakrishnan_4-descent_2003,fisher_improvements_2008,womack_explicit_2003,cremona_minimisation_2010,merriman_explicit_1996}
to compute real approximations of generators of rank 1 elliptic curves,
and incorporated lattice reduction techniques \cite{elkies_rational_nodate}
into the computational pipeline. Leveraging this integrated method,
Watkins successfully calculated the generator of an elliptic curve
with a canonical height of approximately 12557, with the entire computation
taking only half a day under the hardware conditions available at
that time --- a remarkable improvement in efficiency compared to
the pure Heegner point method. 

Building on Watkins\textquoteright{} seminal work, this paper presents
a Pari/GP implementation of the combined Heegner point and 4-descent
method for computing generators of rank 1 elliptic curves. The complete
source code for this implementation is openly available on GitHub\cite{ellheegner4d},
aiming to provide a practical and accessible computational tool for
researchers working on elliptic curve arithmetic.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Algorithm Overview}

To compute the generators of rank 1 elliptic curves efficiently, a
combined method based on Heegner points and 4-descent is adopted,
which is derived from Watkins' work in 2006 and implemented using
a slightly modified version of Pari/GP. The specific implementation
steps of the method are detailed as follows: 

First, the $\texttt{ellheegner}$ function in Pari/GP is modified
to obtain a new function $\texttt{ellheegner\_z}$, whose input parameters
are an elliptic curve $E$ (the target curve for generator computation)
and a binary precision $H$. The value of $H$ is determined by the
canonical height $h$ of the generator, and it generally satisfies
the relation $H=\left\lfloor \frac{h}{12\log2}\right\rfloor $. The
$\texttt{ellheegner\_z}$ function returns a lattice point $z$, using
the $\texttt{ellztopoint}$ function provided in Pari/GP, the real
form corresponding to the generator of curve $E$ can be derived from
$z$.

Next, the online Magma computational tool\cite{magma} is utilized
to compute the 2-cover $D$ and 4-cover $F$ of the elliptic curve
$E$. Let $\xi$ denotes the 2-covering map from $E$ to $D$, and
$\phi$ denotes the map from $D$ to $F$. Based on these two maps
$\xi$ and $\phi$, a real point $X$ on the 4-cover $F$ is computed
using the rational point $P_{0}$ on $E$. This real point $X$ can
be expressed in the form $X=(1,x_{0},y_{0},z_{0})$, where $x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}$
are all real numbers. It should be noted that the same rational point
$P_{0}$ usually yields 4 different real points $X$, all of which
need to be verified one by one in the subsequent computational steps
to ensure correctness.

Subsequently, a matrix $M_{4}$ is constructed using the real point
$X$ computed above. The lattice reduction method is applied to matrix
$M$ to obtain a new integer matrix. The product of this integer matrix
and the vector $[1,0,0,0]$, denoted as $X_{1}$, is taken as the
candidate rational point on the 4-cover $F$. Verifying whether $X_{1}$
is a true rational point on $F$ can be easily achieved through simple
calculations.

An important note is that the lattice point $z$ directly returned
by $\texttt{ellheegner\_z}$ cannot be used directly in the above
computation process. In addition to the lattice point $z$, the $\texttt{ellheegner\_z}$
function also returns the real period $\Omega_{r}$, complex period
$\Omega_{m}$ of the elliptic curve $E$, and a positive integer $K$.
We define a new lattice point $\ensuremath{z_{1}}$ as 

\begin{equation}
z_{1}=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
\frac{-z+k\Omega_{r}}{K} & N<0\\
\frac{-z+k\Omega_{r}}{K}+\frac{\Omega_{m}}{2} & N>0
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $\ensuremath{k}$ is an integer parameter. To obtain a valid
rational point on $F$, we traverse the integer $k$ in the range
of $0$ to $K$, and for each $k$, we repeat the aforementioned computational
process until the corresponding $z_{1}$ yields a true rational point
on $F$.

\subsection{2-descent}

Consider the quartic curve $D$ defined by $y^{2}=ax^{4}+bx^{3}+cx^{2}+dx+e$,
where $a,b,c,d,e$ are coefficients of the quartic polynomial. Two
key invariants $I$ and $J$ associated with the quartic curve $D$
are defined as follows: 
\begin{align}
I= & 12ea-3db+c^{2}\\
J= & \left(72ec-27d^{2}\right)a-27eb^{2}+9dcb-2c^{3}
\end{align}

The quartic curve $D$ is isomorphic to the elliptic curve $E_{I,J}$,
which is given by:

\begin{equation}
Y^{2}=X^{3}-27IX-27J
\end{equation}

The 2-covering map $\xi:D\to E$ is explicitly expressed as follows,
where $g_{4}$ and $g_{6}$ are auxiliary polynomials constructed
from the coefficients of $D$, and their specific forms are defined
by the coefficients $\ensuremath{A_{n}}$(for $g_{4}$) and $B_{n}$
(for $g_{6}$):

\begin{eqnarray*}
g_{4} & = & \sum_{n=0}^{4}A_{n}x^{4-n}\\
g_{6} & = & \sum_{n=0}^{6}B_{n}x^{6-n}
\end{eqnarray*}

The coefficients $A_{n}$ ( $n=0,1,2,3,4$ ) are:

\begin{eqnarray*}
A_{0} & = & 3b^{2}-8ca,\\
A_{1} & = & -24da+4cb,\\
A_{2} & = & 4c^{2}-48ea-6db,\\
A_{3} & = & 4dc-24eb,\\
A_{4} & = & 3d^{2}-8ec
\end{eqnarray*}

The coefficients $B_{n}$ ( $n=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ ) are:

\begin{eqnarray*}
B_{0} & = & 8da^{2}-4cba+b^{3},\\
B_{1} & = & 32ea^{2}+\left(4db-8c^{2}\right)a+2cb^{2},\\
B_{2} & = & \left(40eb-20dc\right)a+5db^{2},\\
B_{3} & = & 20eb^{2}-20d^{2}a,\\
B_{4} & = & \left(20ec-5d^{2}\right)b-40eda,\\
B_{5} & = & 8ec^{2}-32e^{2}a-4edb-2d^{2}c,\\
B_{6} & = & 4edc-8e^{2}b-d^{3}
\end{eqnarray*}

Finally, the 2-covering map $\xi$ maps a point $(x,y)\in D$ to a
point $(X,Y)\in E$ via the following transformation (where $y\neq0$
to ensure the rationality of the map):

\begin{equation}
\left(X,Y\right)=\left(\frac{3g_{4}}{\left(2y\right)^{2}},\frac{27g_{6}}{\left(2y\right)^{3}}\right)
\end{equation}


\subsection{4-descent }

Let $\ensuremath{f_{1}}$ and $f_{2}$ denote two quadric polynomials
in four variables $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}$ (where $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}$
are the independent variables of the quadrics). Let $\bm{P}$ and
$\bm{Q}$ be the Hessian matrices of $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$ respectively.
Let $X$ be a set of rational points that satisfy both quadric equations
$f_{1}=0$ and $f_{2}=0$. The map $\ensuremath{\phi}$ from the 4-cover
to the curve $D$ is defined as follows, with detailed explanations
of each variable and symbol provided: 

First, the elements of the Hessian matrices $\bm{P}$ and $\bm{Q}$
are defined by the second-order partial derivatives of $f_{1}$ and
$\ensuremath{f_{2}}$ respectively, where $P_{i,j}$ and $Q_{i,j}$
represent the elements in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column of $\ensuremath{\bm{P}}$
and $\bm{Q}$ ( $i,j=1,2,3,4$ ):

\begin{equation}
P_{i,j}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f_{1}}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}},\quad Q_{i,j}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}f_{2}}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}
\end{equation}

Next, expand the determinant of the linear combination of matrices
$\bm{P}t+\bm{Q}$ into a polynomial in $t$, where $\sigma_{n}$ (
$n=0,1,2,3,4$ ) denote five coefficients of the polynomial which
is written as:

\begin{equation}
\det\left(\bm{P}t+\bm{Q}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{4}\sigma_{n}t^{4-n}
\end{equation}

Let $\text{adj}(\cdot)$ denote the adjugate matrix of a square matrix.
The adjugate of the linear combination of the adjugate matrices $\text{adj}(\bm{P})t+\text{adj}(\bm{Q})$
satisfies the following relation, where $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ are
intermediate auxiliary matrices introduced to simplify the expression
:

\[
\text{adj}\left(\text{adj}\left(\bm{P}\right)t+\text{adj}\left(\bm{Q}\right)\right)=\sigma_{0}^{2}\bm{P}t^{3}+\sigma_{0}d_{1}t^{2}+\sigma_{4}d_{2}t+\sigma_{4}^{2}\bm{Q}
\]

Define two symmetric matrices $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ by matrix multiplication, 

\[
F_{1}=X\cdot d_{1}\cdot X^{T},\quad F_{2}=X\cdot d_{2}\cdot X^{T}
\]

Let $G$ be a scalar quantity satisfying the following quadratic equation,
where the right-hand side is a polynomial in $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$
constructed using coefficients $\sigma_{n}$:

\[
G^{2}=\sum_{n=0}^{4}\sigma_{n}\left(-F_{1}\right)^{4-n}F_{2}^{n}
\]

Finally, the map $\phi$ from any rational point $(x,y)$ on the 4-cover
to the corresponding point on curve $D$ 
is given by the following coordinate transformation (where $F_{2}\neq0$
to ensure the rationality of the transformation):

\[
\left(x,y\right)\rightarrow\left(-\frac{F_{1}}{F_{2}},\frac{G}{F_{2}^{2}}\right)
\]


\subsection{4-descent Computation Via MAGMA}
The computation relies on the built-in functions \texttt{TwoDescent} and \texttt{FourDescent}, which implement the standard 2-descent and 4-descent algorithms for elliptic curves. The explicit MAGMA code and corresponding output are presented below.
\\ \\ 

% MAGMA 计算代码
\begin{lstlisting}[caption={MAGMA code for 4-descent computation}]
E := EllipticCurve([0, 0, 1, -5115523309, -140826120488927]);
T2 := TwoDescent(E);
T4 := FourDescent(T2[1]);
T4;
\end{lstlisting}

% 运行输出结果
\begin{lstlisting}[caption={Output of the 4-descent computation}]
[
    Curve over Rational Field defined by
    $.1*$.2 + 3*$.1*$.4 + 4*$.2^2 + 5*$.2*$.3 - 5*$.2*$.4 + 7*$.3^2 + 10*$.3*$.4
        + 8*$.4^2,
    3*$.1^2 - 27*$.1*$.2 + 29*$.1*$.3 - 10*$.1*$.4 + 11*$.2^2 - 9*$.2*$.3 -
        4*$.2*$.4 + 8*$.3^2 + 10*$.3*$.4 + 3*$.4^2
]
\end{lstlisting}

\subsection{Matrix and Derivatives Computation for Lattice Reduction}

Given a real point $(1,x_{0},y_{0},z_{0})$ on the 4-cover $F$ and
a bound $B$, the matrix $M_{4}$ is defined as:
\[
M_{4}=\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
1 & -x_{0}B & \left(y^{'}x_{0}-y_{0}\right)B^{2} & \left(-e\left(y^{'}x_{0}-y_{0}\right)+z^{'}x_{0}-z_{0}\right)B^{3}\\
0 & B & -y^{'}B^{2} & \left(ey^{'}-z^{'}\right)B^{3}\\
0 & 0 & B^{2} & -eB^{3}\\
0 & 0 & 0 & B^{3}
\end{array}\right)
\]
where $e=\frac{z^{''}}{y^{''}}$, with $y''$ and $z''$ being the
second-order derivatives of $y$ and $z$ with respect to $x$ (evaluated
at $x=x_{0}$). 

To compute $\ensuremath{y'},\ensuremath{z'},\ensuremath{y''}$, and
$z''$ (all at $x=x_{0}$), we define auxiliary functions 
\begin{eqnarray*}
f_{3}\left(x,y,z,y^{'},z^{'}\right) & = & \frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial y}y^{'}+\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial z}z^{'}\\
f_{4}\left(x,y,z,y^{'},z^{'}\right) & = & \frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial y}y^{'}+\frac{\partial f_{2}}{\partial z}z^{'}
\end{eqnarray*}
which satisfy 

\[
\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
f_{3}\left(x,y,z,y^{'},z^{'}\right) & =0\\
f_{4}\left(x,y,z,y^{'},z^{'}\right) & =0
\end{array}\right.
\]
solving this system yields $\left.y^{'}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$ and $\left.z^{'}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$. 

For the second-order derivatives, we solve the linear system 
\[
\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
\frac{\partial f_{3}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial f_{3}}{\partial y}y^{'}+\frac{\partial f_{3}}{\partial z}z^{'}+\frac{\partial f_{3}}{\partial y^{'}}y^{''}+\frac{\partial f_{3}}{\partial z^{'}}z^{''} & =0\\
\frac{\partial f_{4}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial f_{4}}{\partial y}y^{'}+\frac{\partial f_{4}}{\partial z}z^{'}+\frac{\partial f_{4}}{\partial y^{'}}y^{''}+\frac{\partial f_{4}}{\partial z^{'}}z^{''} & =0
\end{array}\right.
\]
by substituting $\left.y^{'}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$ and $\left.z^{'}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$,
obtaining $\left.y^{''}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$ and $\left.z^{''}\right|_{x=x_{0}}$.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Computational Efficiency Comparison}
To evaluate the computational efficiency of the proposed method, we take the elliptic curve defined by the Weierstrass equation:
\begin{equation*}
y^2 + y = x^3 - 5115523309x - 140826120488927
\end{equation*}
Its canonical height is around 12557, and the 4-descent of this curve is given by the following two quadric equations:

\begin{eqnarray*}
    0&=&x_1x_2 + 3x_1x_4 + 4x_2^2 + 5x_2x_3 \\
    &&- 5x_2x_4 + 7x_3^2 + 10x_3x_4 + 8x_4^2 \\
    0&=&3x_1^2 - 27x_1x_2 + 29x_1x_3 - 10x_1x_4 + 11x_2^2\\
    & &- 9x_2x_3 - 4x_2x_4 + 8x_3^2 + 10x_3x_4 + 3x_4^2
\end{eqnarray*}

All computations are performed on a computer equipped with an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Silver 4210R CPU @ 2.40GHz (running at 3.2GHz) and 128GB of RAM. The computational time consumed by different software and functions is summarized in Table \ref{tab:computational_time}.
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Computational Time Comparison}
\label{tab:computational_time}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\hline
Software & Function & Time \\
\hline
    Pari/GP & \texttt{ellheegner} & 16h, 46min, 13,750 ms \\
    Pari/GP & \texttt{ellheegner4d} & 1h, 26min, 53,649 ms \\
    MAGMA   & \texttt{HeegnerPoints} & 2h, 29min, 39,700 ms \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

In the MAGMA computational environment, the \texttt{HeegnerPoints} function can be integrated with the 4-descent method for generator computation, and the specific implementation code is provided as follows. 

\begin{lstlisting}[caption={MAGMA code for 4-descent and HeegnerPoints computation}]
E := EllipticCurve([0,0,1,-5115523309,-140826120488927]);
T2 := TwoDescent(E);
T4 := FourDescent(T2[1]);
P  := HeegnerPoints(T4[1]);
P;
\end{lstlisting}
It should be noted that the \texttt{HeegnerPoints} function (in MAGMA) and the \texttt{ellheegner4d} function (in Pari/GP) represent two different implementations of the same underlying method. Quantitative analysis indicates that \texttt{ellheegner4d} achieves a computational efficiency improvement of more than 50\% compared to \texttt{HeegnerPoints}. Furthermore, in contrast to the traditional \texttt{ellheegner} function (in Pari/GP), the \texttt{ellheegner4d} function is more than 10 times faster.

\subsection{A Computational Example}
To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for computing
generators of rank 1 elliptic curves with high canonical heights,
we select an elliptic curve from the Stein and Watkins database \cite{goos_database_2002,stein_httpsgithubcomsagemathdatabase_stein_watkins_nodate}.
The curve is defined by the following Weierstrass equation: 

\[
y^{2}+y=x^{3}-x^{2}-636884234186034-6186412091784687672887
\]

. The first derivative of the $L$-series of $E$ at $s=1$ is $L'(E,1)=44.9991292873\cdots$,
and the $\texttt{ellbsd}$ function in Pari/GP yields $c=0.000950351862\cdots$.
The canonical height of the generator of $E$ is calculated as the
ratio of these two values:

\[
\frac{L^{'}\left(E,1\right)}{c}=47349.97007139\cdots
\]

This confirms that the curve has a high canonical height (approximately
47349), which is challenging to compute using the traditional Heegner
point method alone. Next, we perform 4-descent computation for this
curve, and the corresponding quadric equations defining the 4-cover
$F$ are given by:

\begin{eqnarray*}
0 & = & 18x_{1}^{2}+14x_{1}x_{2}+7x_{1}x_{3}+12x_{1}x_{4}\\
 &  & -18x_{2}^{2}-40x_{2}x_{3}-20x_{2}x_{4}+28x_{3}^{2}\\
 &  & -21x_{3}x_{4}+35x_{4}^{2}\\
0 & = & 17x_{1}^{2}-23x_{1}x_{2}+10x_{1}x_{3}+56x_{1}x_{4}\\
 &  & +67x_{2}^{2}+14x_{2}x_{3}+107x_{2}x_{4}+40x_{3}^{2}\\
 &  & -35x_{3}x_{4}-34x_{4}^{2}
\end{eqnarray*}
Using the modified $\texttt{ellheegner\_z}$ function in Pari/GP,
we obtain the following key outputs for the curve $E$: 
\begin{eqnarray*}
z & = & 0.00043328006\cdots\\
\Omega_{r} & = & 0.00047517593\cdots\\
\Omega_{m} & = & 0.00023758\cdots-i\cdot0.0043779\cdots\\
K & = & 48
\end{eqnarray*}

Following the computational steps detailed in Section 2.5, we further
obtain a rational point $X=(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4})$ on the 4-cover
$F$ via 
$z_1 = \frac{-z+46\Omega_r}{48}$. Finally, by verifying and transforming this rational point,
we derive the generator of the elliptic curve $E$, which is of the
form $\left(\frac{p}{q^{2}},\frac{r}{q^{3}}\right)$ . The values
of $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},p,q,r$ are listed in the Appendix 2.

\section{Conclusion}

This paper presents a computational method for computing generators
of rank 1 elliptic curves, which combines the Heegner point method
and 4-descent method and is implemented based on a modified version
of Pari/GP. The effectiveness of the method is verified by successfully
computing the generator of an elliptic curve with a canonical height
of approximately 47349, which is difficult to achieve using the traditional
Heegner point method alone. The related code has been open-sourced
on GitHub, providing a practical tool for researchers in the field
of elliptic curve arithmetic. For future research, we can explore
the combination of the Heegner point method and the 6-descent method,
which is expected to further improve the computational efficiency
for elliptic curves with higher canonical heights and larger conductors.
Additionally, optimizing the existing code to reduce computational
time and expand the scope of applicable curves can be another important
research direction.
